query: offline policy evaluation support overlap positivity assumption limited support confidence bound cross fitting reinforcement learning
content:
**Offline Policy Evaluation (OPE)** in reinforcement learning estimates the value (expected cumulative reward) of a target policy π_e using only offline data collected by a (possibly different) behavior policy π_b, without further environment interaction. [[1]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.06355)

Key challenges include **distribution shift** (actions/states under π_e may differ from the data), high variance in estimators, and the need for statistical guarantees like confidence bounds.

### Core Assumptions: Support Overlap and Positivity
The **positivity** (or **overlap/common support**) assumption is fundamental. It requires that the support of the target policy π_e is contained within the support of the behavior policy π_b: for every state s, if π_e(a|s) > 0, then π_b(a|s) > 0. [[2]](https://mattlanders.net/off-policy-evaluation.html)

- This ensures the value of π_e is **identifiable** from the observed data distribution.
- Equivalently, the importance weights (likelihood ratios π_e(a|s)/π_b(a|s)) remain finite.
- **Weak positivity** is a slightly relaxed version used in some theoretical analyses. [[1]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.06355)

**Limited support** (or lack of full overlap) violates this and makes unbiased evaluation impossible without additional assumptions. In practice:
- Without overlap, methods often produce high-variance estimates or rely on extrapolation.
- Recent work explores **partial identification** (bounds instead of point estimates) when overlap fails, using non-parametric assumptions on conditional means. [[3]](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Off-policy-evaluation-beyond-overlap%3A-partial-Khan-Saveski/d186f3787e1679211eee8b9b8b37f9228c063764)
- Distributionally robust approaches (e.g., Wasserstein uncertainty sets) handle non-overlapping supports by hedging against worst-case shifts. [[4]](https://optimization-online.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/01/8211.pdf)

**Violation consequences**: Estimators can have exploding variance or bias. Real-world datasets (e.g., healthcare, robotics) frequently have limited overlap due to safety constraints on the behavior policy.

### Common OPE Estimators
1. **Direct Method (DM)**: Learns a model of rewards/transitions and simulates the target policy. Low variance but high bias if the model is misspecified.
2. **Importance Sampling (IS)**: Reweights trajectories by the cumulative importance ratio. Unbiased under positivity but high variance (especially in long horizons).
3. **Doubly Robust (DR)**: Combines DM and IS; consistent if *either* the reward model *or* propensity (behavior policy) model is correct. Often preferred. [[5]](https://edoconti.medium.com/offline-policy-evaluation-run-fewer-better-a-b-tests-60ce8f93fa15)
4. **Weighted variants** (e.g., WIS, SNIPS) and marginalized IS (e.g., DualDICE, CoinDICE) reduce variance. [[6]](https://sites.ualberta.ca/~szepesva/papers/NeurIPS2020_coindice.pdf)

**Cross-fitting** (sample splitting) is commonly used to reduce bias from overfitting nuisance models (e.g., Q-functions or propensities). It splits data into folds, estimates models on one part, and evaluates on the other (and averages). This helps achieve better finite-sample properties and valid confidence intervals. [[7]](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/bba9be4bc526c5d515a9d3c16ccfe138-Paper-Conference.pdf)

### Confidence Bounds and Statistical Guarantees
- **Non-asymptotic confidence intervals** are active research areas, often using concentration inequalities, bootstrapping, or empirical likelihood methods (e.g., CoinDICE). [[6]](https://sites.ualberta.ca/~szepesva/papers/NeurIPS2020_coindice.pdf)
- Finite-sample bounds depend on factors like concentrability coefficients (measuring distribution shift), effective horizon, and function class complexity.
- **Pessimistic** or conservative estimators provide lower bounds (safe for deployment).
- Tools like OPERA blend multiple estimators adaptively for better accuracy and include finite-sample analysis. [[7]](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/bba9be4bc526c5d515a9d3c16ccfe138-Paper-Conference.pdf)

### Cross-Fitting in OPE
Cross-fitting mitigates overfitting in nuisance parameter estimation (Q-functions, behavior policies). It enables:
- Semiparametric efficiency.
- Valid asymptotic confidence intervals.
- Reduced sensitivity to model misspecification.

It is especially useful in doubly robust or augmented estimators.

### Practical Considerations and Limitations
- **When overlap is limited**: Use partial identification, robust MDPs, or policy constraints (e.g., Supported Policy Optimization). Pure extrapolation is risky. [[8]](https://gerben-oostra.medium.com/policy-learning-without-overlap-is-it-possible-c304dec76240)
- **High-dimensional/large action spaces**: Require function approximation; grouping or representation learning helps.
- **Libraries**: SCOPE-RL (Python) for end-to-end offline RL/OPE. [[9]](https://github.com/hakuhodo-technologies/scope-rl)
- **Evaluation pitfalls**: OPE estimates can be unreliable; combine with conservative methods and (if possible) limited online validation.

**Recent trends** (up to 2025–2026): Hybrid methods, distributionally robust OPE, better handling of confounding, and improved blending/meta-estimators for reliability. [[7]](https://papers.nips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/bba9be4bc526c5d515a9d3c16ccfe138-Paper-Conference.pdf)

For implementation, start with doubly robust + cross-fitting under checked positivity (empirically via support diagnostics). In limited-overlap regimes, shift to bounds or robust optimization. Key references include reviews like Uehara et al. (2022) and practical tutorials on IS/DR. [[1]](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.06355)

This framework balances theory (identifiability via positivity/overlap) with practical robustness (cross-fitting, confidence bounds).

[...] 7 Conclusion We propose a novel offline policy evaluation algorithm, OPERA, that leverages ideas from stack generalization to combine many OPE estimators to produce a single estimate that achieves a lower MSE. Though such stacked generalization / meta-learning has been frequently used to create better estimates from ensembles of input methods in supervised learning, to our knowledge this is the first time it has been explored in offline reinforcement learning. One challenge is that unlike in supervised learning, we do not have ground truth labels for offline policy learning. OPERA uses bootstrapping to estimate the MSE for each OPE estimator in order to find a set of weights to blend each OPE’s estimate. We provide a finite sample analysis of OPERA’s performance under mild assumptions,
